SQL Language Specification ISO/IEC 9075 Complete Reference Documentation Chapter 1 Introduction to SQL SQL Structured Query Language is a standardized programming language designed for managing and manipulating relational databases The language was first standardized by ANSI in 1986 and subsequently by ISO in 1987 Since then SQL has undergone numerous revisions with major versions released in 1992 SQL-92 1999 SQL:1999 2003 SQL:2003 2006 SQL:2006 2008 SQL:2008 2011 SQL:2011 2016 SQL:2016 and most recently 2023 SQL:2023 Each revision has added new features and capabilities while maintaining backward compatibility with previous versions The SQL standard defines the syntax and semantics of SQL statements including data definition language DDL data manipulation language DML data control language DCL and transaction control language TCL statements SQL is designed to be declarative meaning that users specify what data they want to retrieve or manipulate rather than how to perform the operations The database management system DBMS is responsible for determining the most efficient way to execute SQL statements using query optimization techniques Chapter 2 Lexical Elements SQL statements are composed of various lexical elements including keywords identifiers literals operators and special characters Keywords are reserved words that have special meaning in SQL such as SELECT INSERT UPDATE DELETE CREATE DROP ALTER TABLE WHERE FROM JOIN ON AND OR NOT NULL TRUE FALSE Keywords are case-insensitive in most SQL implementations although some databases may treat them as case-sensitive Identifiers are names given to database objects such as tables columns indexes views procedures functions and triggers Identifiers must follow specific naming rules they typically must start with a letter and can contain letters digits and underscores The maximum length of identifiers varies by DBMS but is typically 128 or 255 characters Identifiers can be delimited using double quotes or backticks to allow special characters or reserved words to be used as names Literals represent constant values in SQL including numeric literals string literals date and time literals boolean literals and null literals Numeric literals can be integers such as 42 or floating-point numbers such as 3.14159 String literals are enclosed in single quotes such as 'Hello World' and can contain escape sequences for special characters Date and time literals follow ISO 8601 format such as DATE '2024-11-19' or TIMESTAMP '2024-11-19 05:30:00' Boolean literals are TRUE and FALSE while NULL represents the absence of a value Operators in SQL include arithmetic operators addition subtraction multiplication division modulo comparison operators equal not equal less than greater than less than or equal greater than or equal logical operators AND OR NOT string operators concatenation pattern matching set operators UNION INTERSECT EXCEPT and various other specialized operators Comments in SQL can be single-line comments starting with two hyphens -- and extending to the end of the line or multi-line comments enclosed in /* and */ delimiters Comments are ignored by the SQL parser and are used for documentation purposes Chapter 3 Data Types SQL supports various data types for storing different kinds of information Numeric data types include INTEGER INT SMALLINT BIGINT for whole numbers DECIMAL NUMERIC for fixed-precision numbers FLOAT REAL DOUBLE PRECISION for floating-point numbers Character string data types include CHAR CHARACTER for fixed-length strings VARCHAR CHARACTER VARYING for variable-length strings TEXT CLOB for large text objects Binary data types include BINARY VARBINARY BLOB for storing binary data Date and time data types include DATE for dates TIME for times TIMESTAMP for date and time combinations INTERVAL for time intervals Boolean data type BOOLEAN stores TRUE FALSE or NULL values Some databases also support specialized data types such as JSON XML UUID ARRAY geometric types network address types and user-defined types Chapter 4 Expressions and Predicates Expressions in SQL combine values operators and functions to produce results Value expressions can be column references literal values parameter markers function calls subqueries or complex expressions involving multiple operators Numeric expressions support standard arithmetic operations with operator precedence following mathematical conventions String expressions support concatenation using the || operator or CONCAT function substring extraction using SUBSTRING function case conversion using UPPER and LOWER functions trimming using TRIM LTRIM RTRIM functions and pattern matching using LIKE operator with wildcards percent sign for zero or more characters underscore for single character Date and time expressions support extraction of components using EXTRACT function arithmetic operations on dates and times using INTERVAL values formatting using various format functions and timezone conversions Predicates are expressions that evaluate to TRUE FALSE or UNKNOWN and are used primarily in WHERE clauses HAVING clauses and CHECK constraints Comparison predicates compare two values using operators equals not equals less than greater than less than or equal greater than or equal BETWEEN predicate tests whether a value falls within a range IN predicate tests whether a value matches any value in a list or subquery LIKE predicate performs pattern matching on strings using wildcards NULL predicate tests whether a value is NULL using IS NULL or IS NOT NULL EXISTS predicate tests whether a subquery returns any rows Quantified predicates use ALL ANY SOME with comparison operators and subqueries Logical operators AND OR NOT combine predicates with three-valued logic handling NULL values Chapter 5 Query Expressions The SELECT statement is the primary means of retrieving data from databases A basic SELECT statement consists of SELECT clause specifying columns to retrieve FROM clause specifying tables to query from WHERE clause specifying conditions for filtering rows GROUP BY clause for grouping rows HAVING clause for filtering groups ORDER BY clause for sorting results LIMIT clause for limiting number of rows returned The SELECT clause can include column names expressions aggregate functions window functions and the asterisk wildcard for all columns Column aliases can be specified using AS keyword or simply by following the expression with the alias name The FROM clause specifies one or more tables views or subqueries to retrieve data from Multiple tables can be joined using various join types INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables LEFT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from left table and matching rows from right table RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns all rows from right table and matching rows from left table FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables CROSS JOIN returns Cartesian product of both tables Join conditions are specified using ON clause or USING clause for natural joins The WHERE clause filters rows based on predicates and can include complex conditions combining multiple predicates with logical operators Subqueries can be used in WHERE clause for correlated or non-correlated filtering The GROUP BY clause groups rows that have the same values in specified columns Aggregate functions COUNT SUM AVG MIN MAX are applied to each group The HAVING clause filters groups based on aggregate conditions The ORDER BY clause sorts the result set by one or more columns in ascending ASC or descending DESC order NULL values are sorted either first or last depending on database configuration Window functions perform calculations across sets of rows related to the current row without collapsing the result set like aggregate functions Window functions include ranking functions ROW_NUMBER RANK DENSE_RANK NTILE aggregate functions used as window functions SUM AVG COUNT MIN MAX and value functions LAG LEAD FIRST_VALUE LAST_VALUE Window specifications define the window frame using PARTITION BY for partitioning ORDER BY for ordering and frame clauses ROWS or RANGE for defining frame boundaries Set operations combine results from multiple SELECT statements UNION combines results removing duplicates UNION ALL combines results keeping duplicates INTERSECT returns only rows that appear in both result sets EXCEPT returns rows from first result set that don't appear in second result set Common table expressions CTEs defined using WITH clause provide named temporary result sets that can be referenced within the main query Recursive CTEs allow hierarchical or recursive queries by referencing themselves

Comprehensive Survey of Machine Learning Applications in Database Security and SQL Injection Detection Recent Advances and Future Directions Abstract This comprehensive survey examines the application of machine learning and deep learning techniques to database security with particular focus on SQL injection detection and prevention We systematically review 287 research papers published between 2015 and 2024 across major computer science venues including IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security USENIX Security Symposium Network and Distributed System Security Symposium and various IEEE and ACM journals Our analysis categorizes existing approaches into six main categories traditional machine learning methods including decision trees random forests support vector machines naive Bayes and k-nearest neighbors deep learning approaches including convolutional neural networks recurrent neural networks long short-term memory networks gated recurrent units and transformer-based models ensemble methods combining multiple classifiers hybrid approaches integrating rule-based and learning-based techniques transfer learning methods adapting models across different domains and reinforcement learning approaches for adaptive security We evaluate these approaches across multiple dimensions including detection accuracy measured by precision recall F1-score and area under ROC curve computational efficiency measured by training time inference latency and resource consumption adaptability to new attack patterns measured by performance on zero-day attacks robustness against adversarial examples and evasion techniques scalability to large-scale enterprise deployments and interpretability of model decisions for security analysts Our findings indicate that deep learning models particularly transformer-based architectures achieve highest detection accuracy with F1-scores exceeding 98% on benchmark datasets however these models require substantial computational resources and training data Traditional machine learning methods offer better interpretability and lower computational costs but achieve lower accuracy typically 85-92% F1-scores Ensemble methods provide good balance between accuracy and efficiency achieving 94-96% F1-scores while maintaining reasonable computational requirements We identify several key challenges facing the field including the lack of large-scale diverse labeled datasets for training and evaluation the difficulty of detecting novel attack variants not seen during training the vulnerability of machine learning models to adversarial attacks specifically crafted to evade detection the high false positive rates in production environments leading to alert fatigue the computational overhead of real-time detection in high-throughput systems and the interpretability gap between model predictions and actionable security insights Our survey also examines emerging research directions including few-shot learning for detecting attacks with limited training examples active learning for efficient labeling of security data federated learning for privacy-preserving collaborative model training explainable AI techniques for understanding model decisions automated feature engineering using deep learning graph neural networks for analyzing query structure and relationships continual learning for adapting to evolving attack patterns and quantum machine learning for future security applications We provide detailed analysis of 15 major benchmark datasets used in SQL injection detection research including their size diversity labeling quality and representativeness of real-world scenarios We discuss evaluation methodologies and metrics highlighting common pitfalls such as data leakage between training and test sets unrealistic threat models that don't reflect actual attacker capabilities and evaluation on outdated attack techniques The survey includes comprehensive comparison tables summarizing the performance characteristics implementation details and practical considerations of 50 representative systems from academic research and industry deployments We analyze the gap between research prototypes and production systems identifying factors that hinder technology transfer including scalability limitations integration complexity operational overhead and lack of standardized interfaces Our analysis of industry adoption reveals that while machine learning-based detection is increasingly common in commercial web application firewalls and database security products most deployments use relatively simple models due to operational constraints We examine case studies from major technology companies describing their approaches to SQL injection detection including feature engineering strategies model architectures training procedures deployment configurations and operational experiences The survey discusses the role of machine learning in broader database security context including access control anomaly detection in database activities insider threat detection data leakage prevention and compliance monitoring We explore the integration of SQL injection detection with other security mechanisms such as input validation output encoding parameterized queries web application firewalls and runtime application self-protection We analyze the economic aspects of deploying machine learning-based security systems including development costs infrastructure costs operational costs and return on investment through prevented breaches Our survey identifies best practices for developing and deploying machine learning-based SQL injection detection systems including data collection and labeling strategies feature engineering techniques model selection criteria hyperparameter tuning approaches evaluation methodologies deployment architectures monitoring and maintenance procedures and incident response integration We discuss ethical and legal considerations including privacy implications of collecting and analyzing SQL queries potential for discrimination in automated decision-making liability for false negatives that result in breaches and false positives that block legitimate users and compliance with data protection regulations The survey concludes with research agenda for the field identifying high-priority research questions including how to develop more robust models that resist adversarial attacks how to reduce false positive rates while maintaining high detection accuracy how to create more diverse and representative training datasets how to improve model interpretability for security analysts how to adapt models to new attack techniques with minimal retraining how to scale detection systems to handle millions of queries per second and how to integrate machine learning with other security mechanisms for defense in depth We provide recommendations for researchers including focusing on practical deployability conducting rigorous evaluation using realistic threat models collaborating with industry partners to access production data and sharing code and datasets to enable reproducibility For practitioners we recommend starting with well-established techniques before adopting cutting-edge methods investing in high-quality training data and continuous model updating implementing comprehensive monitoring and alerting maintaining human oversight of automated decisions and participating in information sharing communities to stay current with emerging threats

The Complete History of SQL Injection Attacks From Origins to Modern Sophisticated Techniques A Comprehensive Chronicle 1998 to 2024 The story of SQL injection begins in the late 1990s when the World Wide Web was rapidly expanding and dynamic web applications were becoming increasingly common Jeff Forristal working under the handle Rain Forest Puppy published a groundbreaking article in Phrack Magazine issue 54 titled NT Web Technology Vulnerabilities which documented how attackers could manipulate SQL queries by injecting malicious input through web forms and URL parameters At that time most web developers were building database-driven applications using simple string concatenation to construct SQL queries without understanding the security implications Forristal demonstrated that by entering carefully crafted input containing SQL metacharacters such as single quotes semicolons and comment markers attackers could alter the logic of SQL queries to bypass authentication access unauthorized data modify database contents or even execute arbitrary commands on the database server The initial response from the security community was mixed some dismissed SQL injection as a minor issue affecting only poorly written applications while others recognized it as a fundamental vulnerability that would affect countless systems The year 1999 saw the first widespread awareness of SQL injection as security researchers began discovering vulnerable applications across the internet CERT Coordination Center issued advisories warning about the risks and providing basic mitigation guidance However adoption of secure coding practices was slow as many developers lacked security training and were focused primarily on functionality and time-to-market pressures The early 2000s witnessed the emergence of automated SQL injection tools that made exploitation accessible to less skilled attackers Tools like SQLDict SQLExec and SQLbf automated the process of discovering and exploiting SQL injection vulnerabilities allowing attackers to scan large numbers of websites and compromise databases with minimal effort In 2002 the Open Web Application Security Project OWASP was founded and immediately identified SQL injection as one of the most critical web application security risks including it in the first OWASP Top 10 list published in 2003 The OWASP Top 10 became the industry standard reference for web application security and SQL injection has remained in the list through every subsequent update demonstrating its persistent threat The mid-2000s saw several high-profile SQL injection attacks that brought the issue to mainstream attention In 2005 CardSystems Solutions a payment processing company suffered a massive breach through SQL injection resulting in the compromise of 40 million credit card numbers The breach led to CardSystems losing its ability to process credit card transactions and eventually being acquired by another company The incident highlighted the severe business consequences of SQL injection vulnerabilities and prompted increased scrutiny from payment card industry regulators In 2006 advanced SQL injection techniques began to emerge including blind SQL injection which allows attackers to extract data from databases even when the application doesn't display database errors or query results Blind SQL injection relies on observing application behavior such as response times or subtle differences in page content to infer information about the database Boolean-based blind SQL injection uses true/false conditions to extract data one bit at a time while time-based blind SQL injection uses database sleep functions to create observable delays The year 2007 marked the beginning of large-scale automated SQL injection attacks targeting thousands of websites simultaneously Attackers used botnets to scan the internet for vulnerable sites and automatically inject malicious code into database tables which would then be served to website visitors infecting them with malware These attacks known as mass SQL injection or automated SQL injection affected hundreds of thousands of websites and demonstrated the scalability of SQL injection exploitation In 2008 the Heartland Payment Systems breach occurred which would become one of the largest data breaches in history at that time Attackers used SQL injection to compromise Heartland's payment processing systems and install malware that captured credit card data resulting in the theft of approximately 130 million card numbers The breach cost Heartland over 140 million dollars in settlements fines and remediation expenses and led to the resignation of senior executives The incident prompted significant changes in payment card industry security standards and increased focus on application security testing The late 2000s saw the development of more sophisticated SQL injection techniques including second-order SQL injection where malicious input is stored in the database and later used in a vulnerable query out-of-band SQL injection which uses alternative channels such as DNS queries or HTTP requests to exfiltrate data and SQL injection through HTTP headers cookies and other non-obvious input vectors Researchers also discovered SQL injection vulnerabilities in stored procedures triggers and other database-side code demonstrating that the problem extended beyond web application code In 2009 the concept of SQL injection worms emerged with proof-of-concept demonstrations showing how SQL injection could be used to create self-propagating attacks that spread from one database to another Although large-scale SQL injection worms never materialized in practice the research highlighted the potential for SQL injection to be used in novel attack scenarios The year 2011 brought another major breach when Sony PlayStation Network was compromised through SQL injection affecting 77 million user accounts The breach forced Sony to shut down PlayStation Network for 23 days resulting in massive financial losses estimated at 171 million dollars and severe damage to Sony's reputation The incident led to congressional hearings and increased regulatory scrutiny of data security practices During the early 2010s the security community made significant progress in developing defenses against SQL injection Parameterized queries and prepared statements became widely adopted as the primary defense mechanism Object-relational mapping ORM frameworks that automatically use parameterized queries gained popularity Web application firewalls WAF that can detect and block SQL injection attempts became standard components of enterprise security architectures Static application security testing SAST tools that can identify SQL injection vulnerabilities in source code improved in accuracy and coverage Dynamic application security testing DAST tools that can discover SQL injection vulnerabilities through black-box testing became more sophisticated However despite these advances SQL injection remained a prevalent vulnerability in 2013 the WhiteHat Security Website Security Statistics Report found that 32% of websites had SQL injection vulnerabilities The persistence of SQL injection reflected several factors including the large amount of legacy code that predated secure coding practices the continued use of unsafe coding patterns by developers lacking security training the complexity of modern applications with multiple layers and components and the emergence of new technologies and frameworks that introduced new SQL injection variants In 2014 researchers discovered SQL injection vulnerabilities in popular content management systems e-commerce platforms and enterprise applications demonstrating that even widely-used and supposedly well-tested software could contain SQL injection flaws The year 2015 saw the emergence of NoSQL injection as NoSQL databases like MongoDB Cassandra and CouchDB gained popularity Attackers discovered that many of the same principles that enable SQL injection also apply to NoSQL databases although the specific techniques differ due to different query languages and data models The mid-2010s also witnessed the rise of bug bounty programs where security researchers are rewarded for discovering and reporting vulnerabilities Bug bounty platforms like HackerOne and Bugcrowd revealed that SQL injection remained one of the most commonly reported vulnerability types with researchers earning substantial rewards for finding SQL injection flaws in major technology companies In 2017 the Equifax breach occurred which although primarily attributed to an unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability also involved SQL injection in the attack chain The breach exposed personal information of 147 million people and resulted in costs exceeding 1.4 billion dollars for Equifax The incident led to congressional hearings regulatory investigations and significant changes in data breach notification laws The late 2010s saw increased focus on automated vulnerability discovery using techniques like fuzzing symbolic execution and machine learning Researchers developed tools that could automatically generate SQL injection payloads discover new bypass techniques and identify vulnerabilities in complex applications However attackers also benefited from these advances using automated tools to discover and exploit vulnerabilities at scale In 2019 the Capital One breach occurred where an attacker exploited a web application firewall misconfiguration combined with SQL injection to access data of 100 million customers The breach highlighted that even organizations with sophisticated security programs could fall victim to SQL injection when multiple security controls fail The incident resulted in an 80 million dollar fine from regulators and ongoing legal proceedings The year 2020 brought new challenges as the COVID-19 pandemic forced rapid digital transformation and many organizations quickly deployed new web applications without adequate security testing Security researchers reported a surge in SQL injection vulnerabilities in healthcare applications e-learning platforms and remote work tools The pandemic also saw increased SQL injection attacks targeting organizations perceived as vulnerable during the crisis In 2021 advanced persistent threat APT groups were observed using SQL injection as an initial access vector in sophisticated multi-stage attacks demonstrating that SQL injection remained relevant even in nation-state cyber operations The integration of SQL injection with other attack techniques such as privilege escalation lateral movement and data exfiltration showed the continuing evolution of SQL injection as part of broader attack campaigns The early 2020s also saw the emergence of SQL injection in new contexts including Internet of Things IoT devices cloud-native applications serverless architectures and containerized environments Each of these new technology paradigms introduced unique challenges for SQL injection prevention and detection In 2022 researchers discovered SQL injection vulnerabilities in artificial intelligence and machine learning systems particularly in applications that use natural language processing to generate SQL queries The intersection of AI and SQL injection raised new questions about how to secure systems that dynamically generate code based on user input

Burp Suite Professional Complete User Guide and Reference Manual Version 2024.1 Comprehensive Documentation for Web Application Security Testing Introduction Burp Suite is an integrated platform for performing security testing of web applications developed by PortSwigger Ltd and widely recognized as the industry standard tool for web application penetration testing The suite combines multiple tools that work together seamlessly to support the entire testing process from initial mapping and analysis of an application's attack surface through to finding and exploiting security vulnerabilities Burp Suite is used by security professionals worldwide including penetration testers bug bounty hunters security researchers and developers who need to identify and fix security issues in their applications Installation and Setup Burp Suite Professional requires Java Runtime Environment JRE version 11 or higher to be installed on your system For Windows users download the Windows installer from the PortSwigger website and run the executable which will guide you through the installation process including selecting the installation directory creating desktop shortcuts and configuring file associations For macOS users download the DMG file mount it and drag the Burp Suite application to your Applications folder For Linux users download the JAR file and run it using the java -jar command or use the provided shell script After installation launch Burp Suite and you will be presented with the startup wizard which allows you to create a new project or open an existing one Projects can be stored on disk allowing you to save your work and resume later or you can use a temporary project that exists only in memory Burp Suite supports two types of projects disk-based projects that persist all data to disk and temporary projects that store data in memory only Disk-based projects are recommended for most testing scenarios as they allow you to save your work resume testing sessions and maintain a complete history of your testing activities The next step is configuring Burp Suite to intercept traffic from your browser or application Burp Suite acts as an intercepting proxy sitting between your browser and the target application allowing you to view and modify all HTTP and HTTPS traffic The default proxy listener is configured on localhost port 8080 but you can modify this in the Proxy settings if needed To configure your browser to use Burp Suite as a proxy you need to modify your browser's network settings In Firefox open Settings navigate to Network Settings click Settings under Connection Settings select Manual proxy configuration enter 127.0.0.1 as the HTTP Proxy and 8080 as the Port check the box for Also use this proxy for HTTPS and click OK In Chrome the proxy settings are inherited from the operating system so you need to modify your system proxy settings For Windows open Settings navigate to Network & Internet click Proxy and under Manual proxy setup turn on Use a proxy server enter 127.0.0.1 as the Address and 8080 as the Port and click Save For macOS open System Preferences click Network select your active network connection click Advanced navigate to the Proxies tab check Web Proxy HTTP and Secure Web Proxy HTTPS enter 127.0.0.1 as the Web Proxy Server and 8080 as the port and click OK After configuring your browser proxy you need to install Burp Suite's CA certificate to intercept HTTPS traffic Without the CA certificate your browser will display security warnings for HTTPS sites because it doesn't trust Burp Suite's certificate To install the certificate configure your browser to use Burp Suite as a proxy then navigate to http://burpsuite in your browser This will display the Burp Suite start page where you can click CA Certificate to download the certificate file For Firefox open Settings navigate to Privacy & Security scroll down to Certificates click View Certificates click the Authorities tab click Import select the downloaded certificate file check Trust this CA to identify websites and click OK For Chrome and other browsers that use the system certificate store you need to import the certificate into your operating system's certificate store For Windows double-click the certificate file click Install Certificate select Current User or Local Machine click Next select Place all certificates in the following store click Browse select Trusted Root Certification Authorities click OK and complete the wizard For macOS double-click the certificate file which will open Keychain Access select System or login keychain click Add find the certificate in the list double-click it expand Trust select Always Trust for When using this certificate and close the window Proxy Tool The Proxy tool is the core component of Burp Suite that allows you to intercept view and modify HTTP and HTTPS requests and responses The Proxy tab contains several sub-tabs including Intercept which allows you to intercept and modify individual requests and responses HTTP history which displays all HTTP traffic that has passed through the proxy WebSockets history which displays WebSocket communications and Options which contains various proxy configuration settings The Intercept sub-tab allows you to control whether Burp Suite intercepts requests and responses When interception is enabled Burp Suite will pause each request or response and display it in the Intercept tab allowing you to view and modify it before forwarding it to its destination You can toggle interception on and off using the Intercept is on/off button When a request or response is intercepted you can view its details including the HTTP method URL headers and body You can modify any part of the intercepted message by editing it directly in the text editor After making your modifications you can click Forward to send the modified message to its destination Drop to discard the message or Action to perform various actions such as sending the message to other Burp Suite tools The HTTP history sub-tab displays a complete log of all HTTP traffic that has passed through the proxy Each entry shows the request number time method URL status code length MIME type and other details You can click on any entry to view the full request and response including headers and body The history can be filtered using various criteria such as showing only in-scope items items with specific status codes or items matching specific search terms You can also annotate history items with comments and highlights to help organize your testing The Options sub-tab contains numerous configuration settings for the proxy including proxy listeners which define the interfaces and ports that Burp Suite listens on for incoming connections intercept client requests and intercept server responses which allow you to configure rules for automatically intercepting or forwarding messages based on various criteria response modification which allows you to automatically modify responses such as unhiding hidden form fields or removing JavaScript that interferes with testing match and replace which allows you to define rules for automatically replacing parts of requests or responses and SSL pass through which allows you to configure specific hosts where SSL connections should be passed through without interception Target Tool The Target tool helps you define and organize the scope of your testing and provides detailed information about the target application The Target tab contains two sub-tabs Site map which displays a hierarchical view of all content discovered on the target application and Scope which allows you to define which hosts and URLs are in scope for your testing The Site map displays all URLs that Burp Suite has observed organized in a tree structure by protocol host and path For each item in the site map you can view details including the HTTP request and response the number of requests made to that URL and any issues that have been identified You can expand and collapse branches of the tree to navigate through the application structure The site map can be filtered to show only in-scope items items with specific response codes or items matching specific search terms You can also manually add items to the site map by right-clicking and selecting Add item The Scope sub-tab allows you to define which targets are in scope for your testing Defining scope is important because it allows you to focus on the specific targets you are authorized to test and exclude out-of-scope targets such as third-party sites You can add items to scope by entering URL prefixes or using advanced scope control which allows you to define scope using protocol host port and file patterns You can also add items to scope directly from other Burp Suite tools by right-clicking on requests and selecting Add to scope Burp Suite will prompt you whether to stop logging out-of-scope items which can help reduce clutter in your proxy history and site map Scanner Tool The Scanner tool automatically crawls and scans web applications to identify security vulnerabilities Burp Suite Professional includes an advanced web vulnerability scanner that can detect a wide range of issues including SQL injection cross-site scripting command injection path traversal file inclusion and many others The Scanner tab contains several sub-tabs including Scan queue which displays active and completed scans Issue activity which shows issues as they are discovered Issue definitions which provides detailed information about each type of vulnerability and Options which contains scanner configuration settings To start a scan you can right-click on any item in the site map proxy history or other tool and select Scan or Do active scan or Do passive scan Active scanning sends requests to the application to probe for vulnerabilities and may modify application state while passive scanning only analyzes existing traffic without sending additional requests The Scan queue sub-tab displays all active and queued scans showing the target URL scan type status progress and number of requests made You can pause resume or cancel scans and configure various scan settings such as the scan speed and resource limits The Issue activity sub-tab displays all vulnerabilities discovered by the scanner organized by severity high medium low and informational For each issue you can view detailed information including the issue type description affected URL vulnerability evidence remediation advice and references to additional information You can also mark issues as false positives or add comments to track your testing progress The Scanner Options sub-tab contains extensive configuration settings for controlling scanner behavior including attack insertion points which define where the scanner will inject payloads active scanning optimization which controls the speed and thoroughness of scanning active scanning areas which allows you to enable or disable specific vulnerability checks passive scanning which controls what passive checks are performed and static code analysis which integrates with Burp Suite's JavaScript analysis capabilities Intruder Tool The Intruder tool allows you to perform automated customized attacks against web applications such as fuzzing testing for vulnerabilities and extracting data The Intruder tool is highly flexible and can be used for a wide variety of testing scenarios including brute force attacks testing for SQL injection and XSS extracting useful data from responses and fuzzing for application errors The Intruder tab contains several sub-tabs including Target which specifies the target host and port Positions which defines where payloads will be inserted in the request Payloads which configures the payloads to be used in the attack Options which contains various attack configuration settings and Results which displays the results of the attack To use Intruder you first need to send a request to Intruder by right-clicking on a request in another tool and selecting Send to Intruder The request will appear in the Intruder Target tab showing the target host and port In the Positions tab you define where in the request you want to insert payloads by placing payload markers around the relevant parts of the request Burp Suite will automatically mark common injection points such as parameter values but you can manually add remove or modify payload positions The Positions tab also allows you to select the attack type which determines how multiple payload positions are handled Sniper uses a single payload set and places each payload into each position in turn Battering ram uses a single payload set and places the same payload into all positions simultaneously Pitchfork uses multiple payload sets and places payloads into positions in parallel using one payload from each set per request and Cluster bomb uses multiple payload sets and tries all combinations of payloads across all positions In the Payloads tab you configure the payloads to be used in the attack Burp Suite supports numerous payload types including simple list which uses a predefined list of strings runtime file which loads payloads from a file at runtime custom iterator which generates payloads by combining items from multiple lists character substitution which generates payloads by substituting characters in a base string case modification which generates case variations of a base string recursive grep which extracts payloads from previous responses illegal Unicode which generates various Unicode encodings character blocks which generates strings of a specific character numbers which generates sequential or random numbers dates which generates date values brute forcer which generates all possible strings of a given character set and length null payloads which generates empty payloads username generator which generates common username formats and ECB block shuffler which manipulates encrypted data For each payload type you can configure various settings such as the payload list character set number range or extraction pattern The Options tab contains numerous settings for controlling attack behavior including request headers which allows you to modify headers for each request request engine which controls the number of concurrent requests and timing between requests grep match which extracts and displays specific strings from responses grep extract which extracts data from responses using start and end markers grep payloads which highlights responses containing the payload redirections which controls how redirections are handled and results which controls what information is displayed in the results The Results tab displays the results of the attack showing each request number payload status code error length time and other details You can sort and filter results to identify interesting responses such as those with different status codes lengths or content You can click on any result to view the full request and response and you can mark results with comments and highlights

Comprehensive Performance Benchmark Study of SQL Injection Detection Systems Evaluation Methodology Results Analysis and Recommendations Executive Summary This comprehensive benchmark study evaluates the performance of 32 different SQL injection detection systems including rule-based systems machine learning classifiers deep learning models and hybrid approaches The evaluation uses a diverse dataset of 500,000 SQL queries collected from real-world applications penetration testing tools and security research The study measures multiple performance dimensions including detection accuracy false positive and false negative rates computational efficiency scalability robustness and operational characteristics The results provide valuable insights for security practitioners selecting detection systems and researchers developing new approaches Evaluation Methodology The benchmark evaluation follows a rigorous methodology designed to ensure fair comparison across different system types and provide results that reflect real-world performance The test dataset consists of 500,000 SQL queries with 400,000 benign queries and 100,000 malicious queries The benign queries are collected from production application logs of 50 different web applications spanning e-commerce content management customer relationship management and enterprise resource planning systems The malicious queries include manually crafted injection attacks automated tool-generated payloads and real attack samples from honeypots and incident response cases The dataset is carefully balanced to include diverse query patterns database systems SQL dialects and attack techniques The malicious queries are categorized by attack type including union-based injection boolean-based blind injection time-based blind injection error-based injection stacked queries second-order injection and out-of-band injection Each attack category includes multiple variants with different evasion techniques such as encoding obfuscation and comment insertion The dataset is split into training validation and test sets using stratified sampling to ensure representative distribution across all categories The training set contains 60% of the data used for training machine learning models the validation set contains 20% used for hyperparameter tuning and model selection and the test set contains 20% used for final evaluation All reported results are based on the test set which was never used during model development The evaluation environment consists of dedicated servers with Intel Xeon E5-2680 v4 processors 2.4 GHz 14 cores 28 threads 128 GB DDR4 RAM 1 TB NVMe SSD storage and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS operating system All systems are evaluated on identical hardware to ensure fair comparison The evaluation measures multiple performance metrics including accuracy the proportion of correct predictions precision the proportion of predicted malicious queries that are actually malicious recall also called true positive rate the proportion of actual malicious queries that are correctly detected F1-score the harmonic mean of precision and recall false positive rate the proportion of benign queries incorrectly classified as malicious false negative rate the proportion of malicious queries incorrectly classified as benign area under ROC curve AUC a measure of overall classification performance training time the time required to train the model inference latency the time required to classify a single query throughput the number of queries that can be classified per second memory usage the amount of RAM required during operation and model size the storage space required for the trained model For machine learning and deep learning systems the evaluation includes 10-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times to ensure statistical reliability Results are reported as mean values with standard deviations The evaluation also includes ablation studies to understand the contribution of different components feature engineering techniques and hyperparameters Rule-Based Systems Performance Rule-based systems use predefined patterns and signatures to detect SQL injection attacks These systems include web application firewalls intrusion detection systems and specialized SQL injection detection tools The evaluation includes 8 rule-based systems representing both open-source and commercial products ModSecurity with Core Rule Set CRS version 4.0 achieves accuracy of 87.3% with standard deviation of 1.2% across multiple runs The system demonstrates precision of 82.1% meaning that 17.9% of queries flagged as malicious are actually benign resulting in false positives that may impact legitimate users The recall is 78.5% indicating that 21.5% of actual attacks are not detected leaving significant security gaps The F1-score of 80.3% reflects the balance between precision and recall The false positive rate is 8.9% which translates to approximately 36,000 false alarms per day in a system processing 10 million queries daily The false negative rate of 21.5% means that more than one in five attacks will bypass detection The inference latency is 3.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 312 queries per second on a single CPU core Memory usage is minimal at 45 MB and the rule set size is 2.8 MB PHPIDS version 0.7 achieves lower accuracy of 84.7% with precision of 79.8% and recall of 75.2% The F1-score is 77.4% with false positive rate of 10.3% and false negative rate of 24.8% The inference latency is higher at 5.1 milliseconds per query with throughput of 196 queries per second Memory usage is 67 MB and rule set size is 1.2 MB The higher latency is attributed to more complex regular expression matching and additional preprocessing steps Snort with SQL injection detection rules achieves accuracy of 81.2% with precision of 76.4% and recall of 71.8% The F1-score is 74.0% with false positive rate of 12.1% and false negative rate of 28.2% The inference latency is 2.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 357 queries per second Memory usage is 38 MB and rule set size is 890 KB The relatively better performance in terms of latency is due to optimized pattern matching algorithms Suricata with emerging threats SQL injection rules achieves accuracy of 83.5% with precision of 78.9% and recall of 73.6% The F1-score is 76.2% with false positive rate of 11.4% and false negative rate of 26.4% The inference latency is 3.5 milliseconds per query with throughput of 286 queries per second Memory usage is 52 MB and rule set size is 1.5 MB Custom rule-based system developed specifically for this evaluation using manually crafted rules achieves accuracy of 89.1% with precision of 85.3% and recall of 81.7% The F1-score is 83.5% with false positive rate of 7.2% and false negative rate of 18.3% The inference latency is 4.2 milliseconds per query with throughput of 238 queries per second Memory usage is 78 MB and rule set size is 3.4 MB The improved accuracy comes from more comprehensive rules but at the cost of higher computational overhead Analysis of rule-based systems reveals several patterns First accuracy is limited by the coverage of rules systems can only detect attacks that match predefined patterns Second false positive rates tend to be high because rules often use broad patterns that match legitimate queries Third false negative rates are significant because attackers can evade rules using encoding obfuscation and other techniques Fourth computational efficiency is generally good with low latency and memory usage Fifth these systems require continuous rule updates to detect new attack variants Sixth the effectiveness varies significantly across different attack types with good detection of simple attacks but poor detection of sophisticated evasion techniques Machine Learning Systems Performance Machine learning systems use statistical models trained on labeled data to classify SQL queries as benign or malicious The evaluation includes 12 machine learning systems using various algorithms and feature engineering approaches Decision tree classifier using CART algorithm with maximum depth of 15 and minimum samples per leaf of 10 achieves accuracy of 91.4% with precision of 88.7% and recall of 85.3% The F1-score is 87.0% with false positive rate of 5.8% and false negative rate of 14.7% The training time is 23 seconds on the full training set The inference latency is 0.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 1,250 queries per second Memory usage during inference is 156 MB and model size is 42 MB The decision tree uses 8,347 nodes with average depth of 12.3 Feature importance analysis reveals that the most important features are the presence of SQL keywords union select where the number of SQL operators the ratio of special characters to total characters and the query length Random forest classifier with 200 trees maximum depth of 20 and minimum samples per leaf of 5 achieves accuracy of 94.2% with precision of 91.7% and recall of 89.3% The F1-score is 90.5% with false positive rate of 3.1% and false negative rate of 10.7% The training time is 127 seconds The inference latency is 1.8 milliseconds per query with throughput of 556 queries per second Memory usage is 892 MB and model size is 234 MB The ensemble of 200 trees provides better accuracy than single decision tree but requires more computational resources Feature importance analysis shows similar top features as decision tree with additional importance for n-gram features and parse tree depth Support vector machine SVM with radial basis function RBF kernel gamma of 0.01 and regularization parameter C of 10 achieves accuracy of 92.8% with precision of 90.2% and recall of 87.6% The F1-score is 88.9% with false positive rate of 4.2% and false negative rate of 12.4% The training time is 342 seconds significantly longer than tree-based methods The inference latency is 2.3 milliseconds per query with throughput of 435 queries per second Memory usage is 1,247 MB and model size is 387 MB The SVM uses 12,458 support vectors representing 31.1% of training samples The kernel-based approach provides good generalization but requires substantial memory for storing support vectors Naive Bayes classifier using Gaussian distribution assumptions achieves accuracy of 88.6% with precision of 84.2% and recall of 80.8% The F1-score is 82.5% with false positive rate of 7.9% and false negative rate of 19.2% The training time is only 8 seconds making it the fastest to train The inference latency is 0.6 milliseconds per query with throughput of 1,667 queries per second Memory usage is 89 MB and model size is 12 MB The simplicity of Naive Bayes provides computational efficiency but limits accuracy due to independence assumptions that don't hold for SQL query features K-nearest neighbors KNN classifier with k equals 15 and Euclidean distance metric achieves accuracy of 90.3% with precision of 86.9% and recall of 83.7% The F1-score is 85.3% with false positive rate of 6.4% and false negative rate of 16.3% The training time is negligible as KNN is a lazy learning algorithm The inference latency is 12.7 milliseconds per query significantly higher than other methods with throughput of only 79 queries per second Memory usage is 2,134 MB as the entire training set must be kept in memory and model size is 1,876 MB The high inference latency makes KNN impractical for real-time detection in high-throughput systems Gradient boosting classifier using XGBoost with 300 boosting rounds maximum depth of 8 and learning rate of 0.1 achieves accuracy of 95.7% with precision of 93.4% and recall of 91.8% The F1-score is 92.6% with false positive rate of 2.3% and false negative rate of 8.2% The training time is 89 seconds The inference latency is 1.4 milliseconds per query with throughput of 714 queries per second Memory usage is 456 MB and model size is 128 MB The gradient boosting approach provides the best accuracy among traditional machine learning methods by combining multiple weak learners Feature importance analysis reveals that the most discriminative features are the presence of comment markers the ratio of SQL keywords to total tokens the maximum nesting depth of subqueries and the presence of hexadecimal or Unicode encodings Logistic regression with L2 regularization and regularization strength of 1.0 achieves accuracy of 89.8% with precision of 86.1% and recall of 82.9% The F1-score is 84.5% with false positive rate of 6.7% and false negative rate of 17.1% The training time is 34 seconds The inference latency is 0.5 milliseconds per query with throughput of 2,000 queries per second Memory usage is 67 MB and model size is 8.4 MB The linear model provides interpretable coefficients showing which features contribute positively or negatively to malicious classification The top positive features are the presence of union keyword the presence of comment markers and high ratio of special characters
